title: Architecture Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance + ADRs
author: Asha Patel
body:
Overview

Purpose: This page consolidates Redwood Inference’s cross-cutting architecture and standards that teams must follow when designing, implementing, and operating services. It covers API standards, coding conventions, infrastructure and deployment guidelines, model-serving expectations, observability requirements, performance SLOs, and a summary of recently accepted ADRs.

Scope: Applies to all services and repos owned by Engineering (serving-runtime, infra, platform, SDKs, and customer-facing APIs). Exceptions must be approved via the ADR process.

Principles (short):
- Consistency: APIs and infra should follow common primitives to reduce cognitive load and enable platform tooling.
- Predictability: SLOs and failure modes should be explicit and testable.
- Inspectability: Logs, traces, and metrics must be sufficient to debug production incidents without SSHing into hosts.
- Cost-awareness: Architecture choices must include expected unit economics and ops cost.

1) API Standards
- API surface: All externally consumable APIs (hosted API, internal RPCs used across teams) must use contract-first design. Public REST/HTTP endpoints use OpenAPI v3.1 with a single canonical schema per service stored in the repo at /api/openapi.yaml.
- Versioning: Use path versioning: /v1/... for GA. Breaking changes require a new major path and a migration plan documented in the PR and release notes.
- Request/response shape: Prefer explicit response objects with typed fields rather than free-form maps. Avoid domain-specific polymorphism in top-level responses.
- Error model: Standardize on the following JSON error envelope: {"error": {"code": "string", "message": "string", "details": [ {"type": "string", "info": {}} ]}}. Use HTTP status codes per RFC 7231; prefer 4xx for client errors, 5xx for server errors.
- Pagination: Cursor-based pagination required for endpoints that can return >200 items. Use next_cursor + limit pattern.
- Rate limiting: Public API endpoints must include rate-limit headers (X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset).
- Security: All external endpoints require mTLS or token-based auth (JWT with appropriate claims). Sensitive fields (customer data) must be redacted in logs.

Example API contract snippet (OpenAPI-style excerpt):

```
openapi: 3.1.0
paths:
  /v1/generate:
    post:
      summary: Generate text
      x-owner: serving-runtime
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              $ref: "#/components/schemas/GenerateRequest"
      responses:
        '200':
          description: OK
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: "#/components/schemas/GenerateResponse"
components:
  schemas:
    GenerateRequest:
      type: object
      properties:
        model:
          type: string
        prompt:
          type: string
    GenerateResponse:
      type: object
      properties:
        id:
          type: string
        text:
          type: string
```

2) Coding Standards
- Language-specific guides: Each language repo must include a STYLE.md at the repo root. Core rules (applies to all languages):
  1. Prefer explicit typing for public interfaces.
  2. Keep functions <= 60 lines and classes <= 400 lines unless justified.
  3. All public APIs must have unit tests and type checks in CI.
  4. Do not commit secrets; use Vault/KMS.
- Linting & formatting: Enforce with pre-commit hooks and CI: go fmt/go vet for Go, black/isort/flake8 for Python, prettier/eslint for JS/TS.
- Dependency management: Use dependency pinning and automated PRs for upgrades (dependabot or Renovate). Security-critical dependencies must have CVE checks enabled.
- Review process: PRs > 200 LOC require one additional reviewer and a performance or security sign-off if touching runtime-critical paths.

3) Infrastructure Standards
- IaC: Terraform is the canonical tool for cloud infra. Keep modules under //infra/modules and enforce module review. State is kept in remote backend with locking.
- Environments: Must support dev, staging, prod with identical config via parameterization. No ad-hoc prod-only changes.
- Network: Services must be deployed in VPCs with least privilege security groups. Cross-region traffic should use private links where available.
- Secrets & Key Management: Use cloud KMS/HSM for key management. Secrets are delivered to runtime via a secrets provider (Vault or cloud secret manager) and never written to logs.
- CI/CD: All deploys go through the pipeline with automated canaries (see rollout policy below). Rollbacks must be scriptable.

Essential infra config table (example):
| Resource | Minimum | Notes |
|---------|--------:|------|
| Instance type (gpu) | a100-40gb | Dedicated pools may use qdrant/bsr variants per workload |
| Pod CPU request | 0.5 vCPU | Request <= usage to support bin-packing |
| Pod memory request | 2 GiB | Tune per service |
| Logging retention | 90 days | Shorten by request in privacy-sensitive customers |

4) Model-serving Standards
- Model packaging: Models must include a manifest (model.manifest.json) with fields: model_version, architecture, tokenizer, quantization_profile, max_sequence_length, supported_features. The manifest file format is documented in //eng-serving-runtime/model-onboarding/manifest.md.
- Runtime compatibility: Models are validated in the model-onboarding pipeline (unit tests, perf benchmarks, correctness-evals) before being marked GA.
- Quantization: Supported quantization profiles must be declared in quantization-profiles/ and a recommended profile must be provided per model for CPU/GPU/quantized inference.
- KV cache and batching: Services must expose observability hooks for effective batching and KV cache hit rates (see observability section). Batching configurations should be parameterized via runtime flags and observable in metrics.
- Rollouts: Use canary (5\u201310%) followed by linear ramp (doubling every 10\u201320 minutes) to full traffic. Default automatic rollback if error rate > 1.5x baseline or latency P95 regresses > 25% during rollout window.

Model-serving example manifest (JSON snippet):
```
{
  "model_version": "7.1.0",
  "architecture": "decoder-only",
  "tokenizer": "byte-level-bpe",
  "quantization_profile": "int8-4g",
  "max_sequence_length": 4096,
  "supported_features": ["streaming", "function-calls"]
}
```

5) Observability Standards
- Metrics: All services must emit a standard metric set (prefix: service.<name>.):
  - request_total{route,method,status}
  - request_duration_seconds (histogram, buckets aligned to latency SLOs)
  - error_total{route,code}
  - kv_cache_hit_ratio (for model-serving)
- Tracing: Distributed traces with W3C traceparent. Instrument entry and critical internal spans (model inference, batching, KV fetch).
- Logs: Structured JSON logs at minimum level INFO. Include request_id, route, model_id, customer_id (hashed) and non-sensitive metadata.
- Alerts: Alerting rules defined near-owner dashboards. Typical thresholds: error rate > 0.5% sustained for 5m or P95 latency > 2x SLO for 10m.

6) Performance Standards & SLOs
- Global SLOs (guideline):
  - Hosted inference API: availability 99.95% monthly; P95 request latency (for prompt+first-token) <= 300ms for small models, <= 700ms for large-ctx models under typical load.
  - Dedicated pools (customer SLA): availability 99.9% (contracted); P95 latency per-customer configurable via Dedicated profile.
  - Model-serving throughput: measured in tokens/sec per-GPU; each model onboarding must publish baseline throughput and cost-per-1k-tokens estimate.
- Load testing: New services and major changes require a performance test run (k6/locust) simulating expected production patterns. Test reports are stored under eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/reports/.
- Regression gating: Performance regressions (>10% P95) are a blocking failure for rollouts to production and must be accompanied by a rollback plan and triage runbook.

7) Decision Records (ADRs) \u2014 summary of recent decisions
- ADR-2025-08: Standard API Envelope (owner: Asha Patel) \u2014 Decision: adopt canonical JSON error envelope and OpenAPI-first approach. Rationale: simplifies cross-team clients and tooling. Status: accepted.
- ADR-2025-12: Quantization Profile Standard (owner: Ravi Menon) \u2014 Decision: support int8 and int4 profiles with documented accuracy/latency tradeoffs. Status: accepted.
- ADR-2026-01: Canary Rollout Policy (owner: Maria Gonzalez) \u2014 Decision: default canary 5\u201310% with automated rollback thresholds (error rate and P95 regression). Status: accepted.

| ADR-2026-01 | Rollout Policy | Maria Gonzalez | accepted | /confluence/architecture-and-standards/adr-2026-01-rollout-policy |

8) Governance, Ownership & Exceptions
- Ownership: Each service should declare a Tech Lead and a Pager on call. Architecture team (architecture-and-standards) owns the canonical guides and reviews ADRs.
- Exceptions: To deviate from these standards, file an ADR describing the proposal, alternatives, impact, and mitigation. For temporary exceptions (<=14 days) open an exception ticket and notify the architecture mailing list.

9) Operational runbooks & oncall guidance (summary)
- Incident playbook: detect -> page -> mitigate -> communicate -> RCA. Use the incident template under oncall-and-incident-response/runbooks/incident-process.
- Quick triage checklist: check resource saturation (GPU/CPU), check recent deploys, check KV cache hit rates, check error spikes by route.

Appendix: Examples and snippets
- CI snippet (deploy canary):
```
jobs:
  deploy_canary:
    steps:
      - run: terraform apply -var='traffic_percent=5'
      - run: ./ci/healthcheck.sh --timeout 600
```
- Rolling rollback criteria (example):
  1. Error rate > 1.5x baseline for 5m OR
  2. Latency P95 > 25% above baseline for 10m
If either condition is true, the deploy pipeline must automatically rollback and open an incident ticket.
